title: CrisisBench: Benchmarking Crisis-related Social Media Datasets for Humanitarian Information Processing
venue: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
problem_statement: Dispersed crisis-related social media datasets with inconsistent label taxonomies, noisy near-duplicate content, and lacking standardized splits prevent researchers from comparing models and evaluating progress in crisis informatics tasks.
domain: Crisis informatics and disaster response text processing on social media platforms (Twitter).
theoretical_framework: Domain adaptation and transfer learning in natural language processing, using contextualized transformer representations and event-aware side-constraint conditioning to aggregate multi-event disaster data.
methodology: The authors consolidated eight human-annotated crisis tweet corpora by mapping heterogeneous labels into unified informativeness and humanitarian taxonomies. They filtered exact duplicates via string matching and near-duplicates using bag-of-ngrams cosine similarity with a 0.75 threshold, assigned language tags via the Google Cloud Language Detection API, and created standardized 70/10/20 train/dev/test splits. They benchmarked CNN, fastText, BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and multilingual transformers across monolingual, cross-dataset, event-aware, and multilingual settings.
key_findings: Training models on the consolidated dataset yields superior generalization across individual test datasets and achieves higher overall F1-scores than training on single-source datasets.
Pre-trained transformer models (RoBERTa, BERT, DistilBERT) consistently outperform CNN and fastText architectures, delivering substantial performance gains on minority humanitarian classes.
Duplicate and near-duplicate tweets constitute 20% to 25% of uncleaned crisis datasets, and removing those duplicates prevents data leakage between training and evaluation splits.
Event-aware conditioning via prepended event tokens improves CNN multi-class humanitarian classification F1-score from 0.829 to 0.842.
Evaluating models on multilingual crisis data causes a significant performance drop of approximately 8% in F1-score compared to English-only benchmarks.
scope_and_delimitations: Restricted benchmark evaluations to textual tweet content, excluding image and multimodal inputs.
Focused classification experiments primarily on English-language tweets, treating multilingual evaluations as preliminary baselines.
Evaluated binary informativeness and 11-class humanitarian categorization tasks while excluding disaster event type classification.
Omitted multi-label tweets from the DRD dataset to avoid manual re-annotation for single-label multiclass experiments.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Even after combining the datasets, the imbalance in class distribution seems to persist (last column in Table 4). For example, the distribution of "not humanitarian" is relatively higher (37.40%) than other class labels. In Table 4, we highlighted some class labels, which we dropped in the rest of the classification experiments conducted in this study.
limitations.summary: The consolidated dataset retains substantial class imbalance with dominant non-humanitarian tweets and scarce minority categories. In addition, event-aware training fails to improve transformer models, multi-label instances were dropped rather than re-annotated, and performance drops significantly on multilingual subsets.

generalizability_gap: The benchmark evaluations focus predominantly on English tweets collected exclusively from Twitter between 2010 and 2017, leaving model generalizability to non-English languages, alternative social media platforms, and subsequent disaster events untested.
methodological_gap: Token-prefixing event-aware conditioning failed to improve transformer performance, multi-label instances were discarded rather than modeled via multi-label classification frameworks, and similarity-based deduplication relied on a fixed heuristic threshold.
future_work: Evaluating deeper encoder-decoder architectures such as Google T5 for crisis text classification.
Exploring regularization techniques and fine-tuning strategies to enhance transformer performance in crisis informatics.
Investigating multilingual pretrained models and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer for non-English crisis tweets.
Incorporating disaster event type classification into the consolidated benchmark suite.
Extending event-aware conditioning to multi-attribute tags such as geographic disaster region.
